canonical_question: How does the 1199 °C γ′ solvus temperature of this HESA compare to the stability limit of conventional CMSX-2 alloys?

question_variants.question: How does the 1199 °C γ′ solvus temperature of this HESA compare to the stability limit of conventional CMSX-2 alloys?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The paper provides the γ′ solvus for the specific HESA (1199 °C) but does not provide the solvus temperature for conventional CMSX-2 within the supplied evidence, making a direct comparison impossible based solely on the provided text. Evidence Unit 9aa5c1251eb16dd6 cites a general HESA solvus >1150 °C but does not name CMSX-2.

answers.answer: The γ′ solvus of the HESA in this study is 1199 °C. No data for CMSX-2 solvus is provided in the supplied evidence units.
answers.boundary_limitation: CMSX-2 solvus data not present in supplied evidence
evidence_spans: The design of HESA was also assisted by CALPHAD-based simulation (JMatPro [55] , Ni-alloys database), and the aim is to contain more than 60 vol% of strengthening L1 2 γ′ as commercial Ni-based superalloys.

Furthermore, since the addition of refractory elements can easily promote the formation of detrimental topological-close packed (TCP) phases, the fraction of TCP was designed to be less than 1 vol% while adjusting the refractory additions.

answers.answer: Cited literature indicates HESAs generally have γ′ solvus temperatures above 1150 °C, but does not list the specific value for CMSX-2.
evidence_spans: Previous studies have shown that the γ - γ′ microstructure of HESAs can remain stable against topologically-close-packed (TCP) phase formation from 700 to 1100 °C for at least 500 h [15] , and with enhanced γ′ solvus temperatures above 1150 °C [16] .
Furthermore, HESAs have shown good resistances against high temperature oxidation and corrosion by forming protective Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 , respectively [17] .

source_evidence_spans: the γ′ solvus and solidus temperature are 1199 and 1276 °C, respectively.
